system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2148-03-21 13:50:00 to 2148-03-26 18:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of type 2 diabetes, gastroparesis, and anxiety was admitted for severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and poor glycemic control. She presented with elevated lactate and dehydration, consistent with a gastroparesis flare complicated by hyperglycemia. Imaging showed no acute abnormalities, and her elevated white count and lactate were attributed to metabolic stress. She improved with IV fluids, insulin adjustment, and pain management. Her diet was advanced, and she stabilized. A new insulin regimen was initiated with home nursing support arranged. She was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up plans for diabetes and iron management.
problems: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic autonomic (poly)neuropathy
Morbid (severe) obesity due to excess calories
Elevated white blood cell count, unspecified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve been having really bad stomach pain. It started yesterday—sharp, in the upper middle part. I couldn’t sleep at all last night because of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re going through that. Is it different from your usual pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels similar, but worse. I didn’t throw up or feel nauseous this time, which is different. I just couldn’t eat because it hurt too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your labs and scans. Your white blood cell count is high, and your blood sugar is elevated at 453. But your CT scan didn’t show anything urgent like appendicitis or a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection? I’ve had this pain so many times before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. Your urine showed some signs of irritation, so we started antibiotics just in case. But we also drew blood cultures because of your high white count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have that port in my chest because my veins are hard to access. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we know. The blood cultures were drawn from your port. We’re watching closely because you’ve had a bloodstream infection from it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got preliminary results from your blood cultures. They show coagulase-negative staph—specifically epidermidis, hominis, and lugdunensis. It could be contamination, but we’re treating it seriously.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? I’m not running a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right, you’re not febrile, which is reassuring. But because you have a port and a history of line infections, we’re involving Infectious Disease. They recommend starting daptomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to vancomycin and Bactrim. Is daptomycin safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daptomycin is safe for you. It’s a good alternative. We’ll give it through your port once a day for 10 days. You might feel some itching, but we can give Benadryl to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood cultures are negative. That’s a good sign—the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My stomach pain is still there, but maybe a little less?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—from 24.9 to 20.7. That suggests your body is responding. We still think your pain is related to your gastroparesis or chronic GI issues, not an acute surgical problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement in a few days. Could that be making it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Constipation can definitely worsen abdominal pain, especially with your history. We’ll encourage fluids and fiber, and keep your dicyclomine and metoclopramide going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your white count is now 14.9—still high but trending down. Your blood sugar is better too, around 190.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I finally had a big bowel movement this morning. My stomach feels a lot better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. That likely explains the improvement. We’ll keep encouraging regular bowel habits—hydration, movement, and your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I take a stool softener at home too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t have one on your list now, but we can discuss that with your PCP. For now, focus on diet and staying active as you’re able.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff test came back negative, which is good. No need for additional antibiotics for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bacteria in my blood? Is it gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your repeat blood cultures are negative. That means the daptomycin is working. We’ll continue it for the full 10 days, and arrange for home infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need a nurse to come to my house?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a home health nurse will give you the IV antibiotic daily. You’ll also take Benadryl beforehand to prevent itching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your pain is back to your usual baseline, labs are improving, and no fever. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I’m worried about missing my doctor appointments. I can’t get rides on short notice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The social worker tried to help, but we know it’s hard. Try to schedule appointments with at least three days’ notice, and let your doctor know if pain flares up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? My sugars are still high sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose is not fully controlled. Please check it before meals and at bedtime, and write it down. Bring that log to your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. It’s hard when I’m in pain or tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But even a few days of logs will help your doctor adjust your insulin. We’re keeping your current doses for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve confirmed your home infusion service is set up. They’ll start tomorrow and continue for 10 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I take Benadryl every time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 50 mg about 30 minutes before each infusion. It should help prevent any itching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds? I want to make sure I’m taking them right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your usual medications—metoclopramide, dicyclomine, insulin, omeprazole, tramadol as needed. We’re not changing anything else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my iron? I had an infusion last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding off on iron for now because of the recent infection. Once you finish antibiotics, talk to your doctor about restarting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your vitals are stable, pain is manageable, and labs continue to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thank you for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take Benadryl before each antibiotic, check your sugars, stay hydrated, and try to keep your bowels regular.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And call if I start feeling worse or get a fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call your doctor or go to the ER if you develop fever, chills, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still feeling about the same—much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time, and then you can head home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge paperwork is ready. You’ll receive a copy with all your meds, follow-up, and home care details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, and we hope to see you doing well at your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—home health will call you tonight to schedule the first daptomycin dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set to go. The transport team will take you to your ride in about 30 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Take care of yourself, and don’t hesitate to reach out if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—do you have all your prescriptions and instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, everything’s here. I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of type 2 diabetes, gastroparesis, morbid obesity, and a Port-A-Cath due to difficult venous access was admitted for acute-on-chronic epigastric pain. She presented with leukocytosis (WBC 24.9) and hyperglycemia (glucose 453), but imaging showed no acute abdominal pathology. Blood cultures drawn from her port grew multiple coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species, prompting Infectious Disease consultation and treatment with daptomycin. She remained afebrile, and repeat blood cultures were negative. Her abdominal pain improved significantly after bowel movements, consistent with chronic functional GI issues. She was discharged home on a 10-day course of outpatient daptomycin with home health support, Benadryl premedication, and instructions to monitor blood glucose and maintain bowel regularity.

Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic autonomic (poly)neuropathy
Morbid (severe) obesity due to excess calories
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified
